title: In the Cut
full_review:
You know you are in trouble when you are watching a serial-killer movie and midway through the film you find yourself hoping that the female lead is the psycho's next victim.

Such is the case with "In the Cut" (Screen Gems), an excruciatingly dreadful erotic thriller about a college professor who becomes involved with a New York City homicide detective who is investigating a string of grisly murders.

Thanks to a torpid, unremittingly cheerless script, director Jane Campion's urban-noir tale suffocates under the weight of its own self-importance, quickly plummeting into a soporific fog of pretension and voyeuristic vulgarity.

Meg Ryan stars as Frannie Avery, a romance-wary creative writing teacher living in lower Manhattan who becomes intrigued by the horrific unsolved murder of a young woman that occurred in her neighborhood. Encouraged by her promiscuous, emotionally unhinged half-sister, Pauline (Jennifer Jason Leigh), Frannie begins a salacious relationship with the edgy cop working the case, Detective Molloy (Mark Ruffalo).

Though his unabashed carnality rouses her passions, Frannie remains leery, especially after spying his suspicious wrist tattoo, which may or may not incriminate him in the serial murders. With Molloy as her guide, Frannie embarks on a dangerous journey down the rabbit hole to the heart of sexual darkness, a voyage which involves perils both emotional and physical.
The lugubrious murder-mystery plot is peppered throughout with red-herring characters, including Frannie's intense student (Sharrieff Pugh) and her stalker ex-boyfriend (Kevin Bacon).

Ryan sheds her girl-next-door image -- along with all her clothes and any trace of likeability -- in this misguided attempt to redirect her career to more "serious" roles, a la Halle Berry in "Monster's Ball" (2001). Whereas in "Monster's Ball" the film's controversial sex scene flowed organically from its story and characters -- two people suffering personal tragedy seeking emotional wholeness and interpersonal comfort -- the raw encounters of "In the Cut" serve no real narrative purpose beyond exploiting the nudity of its A-list star.

And while certain viewers may find the explicit nature of both films offensive, the former at least endeavored to shed light on the human condition, while the latter, bereft of dramatic moorings, seems gratuitous and pornographic.

In the film, based on the best seller by Susanna Moore, Campion purports to use the book's thriller format to explore personal vulnerability and the mystery of human sexuality, but the end result is neither insightful nor thrilling. The film unspools clumsily like a B-movie hiding behind a patina of atmospheric moodiness and Ryan's star power. It is quite ironic that a film centered on a creative writing teacher can be so thoroughly unoriginal and dull.

Mistaking sleaze for substance, the film tries to justify its lewd banality under a pretense of faux weightiness, disguising the poverty of its script with raunchy sex scenes and pretentious dialogue, most of which would be laughable if the script wasn't so unnecessarily coarse.

"In the Cut" does achieve gravity on one level; like a force of nature it succeeds in pulling viewers down -- right into the gutter.

Due to recurring explicit sexual encounters with extended full nudity, including depictions of oral sex and masturbation, several scenes of gory violence, and much rough and sexually crude language, as well as profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
